detail.title: Designed for Whom? Spatial Inequity, Settlement Dynamics, and Newcomer Exclusion from Community Circular Economy Infrastructure
detail.abstract: Community circular economy systems-repair cafés, tool libraries, reuse hubs-are increasingly integrated into municipal waste-diversion strategies. Yet these systems tend to be spatially, informationally, and culturally configured around an implicit default participant: a mobile, English-proficient, environmentally networked resident whose relationship to sustainability is one of voluntary choice. This paper argues that when such assumptions go unexamined, circular infrastructure can reproduce participation inequities regardless of intent. Using a sequential mixed-methods design rooted in participatory action research (PAR), we examine newcomer exclusion from community repair infrastructure in the Greater Toronto Area as a case study in this broader dynamic. Phase 1 exit surveys (N = 200) and GIS spatial mapping document structural friction points-information siloing, multi-modal transit burdens, and a pronounced spatial mismatch between venue locations and newcomer residential density. Targeted 'pop-up' repair events codesigned with settlement agencies served as the PAR intervention. Phase 3 semi-structured interviews with newcomer attendees (n = 20) and volunteer fixers (n = 10) generate three core themes: (1) the consumptionstatus paradox, in which purchasing new goods functions as a settlement milestone that competes with repair culture; (2) the dignity of the fixer, in which underemployed immigrant professionals recover technical agency and professional recognition through volunteer expertise; and (3) structural information siloing that insulates mainstream sustainability networks from newcomer communities. OLS regression confirms that transit complexity, venue familiarity, and language concern are the strongest predictors of attendance hesitancy, with venue type (pop-up vs. established) accounting for the largest explained variance. We propose an Inclusive Circularity framework that treats immigration trajectory, material culture, and settlement infrastructure as first-order design variables rather than post-hoc equity corrections-a reorientation with implications for circular economy governance beyond the repair context.

detail.title: US Monetary Spillovers, Foreign Exchange, and Gold Reserves at Times of Geopolitical Fragmentation

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper studies the role of foreign exchange and gold reserves in mitigating the US monetary policy spillovers to exchange rates at times of geopolitical fragmentation and de-dollarization. US dollar reserves mitigate depreciation driven by US monetary tightening, while non-dollar reserves do not. Gold reserves are also associated with smaller exchange-rate responses, though less strongly than dollar reserves, suggesting novel complementarity between dollar and gold reserves. Moreover, the estimated effects of dollar and gold reserves are concentrated in countries without swap and repo lines. These findings are consistent with recent large-scale purchases and sales of gold reserves by emerging economies amid sanctions-related restrictions and geopolitical concerns about access to dollar liquidity. Our results suggest that not only the aggregate volume but also the composition of foreign exchange and gold reserves and access to dollar liquidity facilities are empirically relevant for exchange-rate responses to US monetary shocks. Finally, we exploit cross-country heterogeneity and show that countries with large dollar exposure exhibit smaller exchange-rate responses when dollar and gold reserve holdings are larger.

detail.abstract:
Rising elderly life expectancy is a well-known source of fiscal pressure on Social Security and Medicare – but how have declining mortality and morbidity affected the two programs’ relative finances? Using nearly three decades of Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey data (1992-2019), we estimate that these demographic changes raised expected lifetime Social Security spending by over twice as much as expected lifetime Medicare spending: 14% compared to 6%. The slower growth of elderly lifetime health care spending than annuity spending reflects two features of how longevity has increased: the additional 2.4 years of remaining life expectancy were entirely healthy – free of physical or cognitive limitations – while the expected amount of time spent with severe health limitations fell by about 30%, reducing expected lifetime nursing-home and home-health use. We then write down a stylized life-cycle model of a risk-averse retiree facing stochastic mortality and health to illuminate the key forces that affect the optimal allocation of a fixed amount of public funds across Medicare and Social Security.

title: AI Diffusion Gaps: Unequal Integration of AI Across K-12 Schools
affiliations: University of Chicago Booth School of Business and University of Rochester - Department of Economics

detail.title: AI Diffusion Gaps: Unequal Integration of AI Across K-12 Schools

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Although use of generative AI tools has quickly become widespread in education settings, emerging evidence suggests that effects on learning will depend on how that use is supported and guided. This paper reports findings from an original national survey of K-12 school principals designed to measure institutional integration of AI in schools through policies, teacher training, guidance for student use, leadership engagement, and the availability of AI-enabled tools. We find that AI use has spread rapidly across schools, largely as a productivity aid. Students mainly use AI for homework help and writing, while educators primarily use it for lesson planning and administrative tasks. The development of teacher training, guidance, and school policies has lagged adoption. We next document two diffusion gaps across schools: First, lower AI integration is associated with a higher share of disadvantaged students (a one standard deviation increase in disadvantage is associated with a 0.07-0.11 SD lower score on an index of AI integration); Second, private and charter schools score 0.23-0.44 SD lower on the AI integration index than traditional public schools. Although several surveyed school-level factors strongly predict AI integration, they do little to explain these gaps. Differences in district size account for roughly one-third of the disadvantage gap between public schools. These findings suggest that the factors associated with greater AI integration differ from those needed to narrow disparities in how schools support and guide AI use.

title: The Informed Insider: A Leading Measure of Quality
affiliations: Columbia Business School, Harvard University - Accounting & Control Unit, ,  and Columbia University in the City of New York

detail.title: The Informed Insider: A Leading Measure of Quality

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Product and service quality is fundamental to firm value creation, yet it is well recognized as difficult to observe ex ante. Existing quality proxies are limited in coverage, lack cross-firm comparability, and primarily rely on lagging indicators that capture product or service failures only after they materialize. Exploiting employees’ informational advantage as informed insiders and firsthand observers of firms’ internal operations, we develop and validate a novel, forward-looking measure of firm-year-level product and service quality using over 4.3 million employee reviews on Glassdoor. Leveraging machine learning models trained on a subset of firms with third-party customer satisfaction data, we construct quality indices for S&P 1500 firms spanning 2008 to 2023. The resulting quality measures exhibit meaningful variation across firms and within firms over time. In out-of-sample tests, our quality indices demonstrate strong predictive power for future quality provision, emerging as the single most important predictor relative to firm fundamentals and Glassdoor ratings. We validate our measure by examining its association with alternative quality metrics. We show that our quality measures are useful in predicting important quality-related firm outcomes such as product recalls, brand value, and profitability. We also construct an alternative set of quality measures using a zero-shot prompt-based approach and a supervised fine-tuning approach with GPT models to assess the potential of LLMs and generative AI in capturing firm-level quality provision. Our paper shows the value of employee voices as a powerful, forward-looking, and scalable signal of firm quality provision. The paper offers implications for stakeholders seeking to identify quality-related risks and opportunities before they become externally visible.

title: Planning Capital and Discovery-Based Learning-by-Doing: Investment as Staged Discovery in the Hyperscale Era
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Planning Capital and Discovery-Based Learning-by-Doing: Investment as Staged Discovery in the Hyperscale Era

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper treats frontier investment as staged discovery. Firms invest through sequences of costly inquiry stages before deciding whether and how to realize value. At each stage, a firm may sharpen its diagnostic understanding, choose what question to ask, embody that question in a costly action, and interpret the answer that action produces. The answer changes what the firm knows, what it can do next, and how costly future inquiry will be. Successful histories can also carry over to later related problems, making the firm a better learner beyond the current investment path.The paper calls the resulting asset planning capital in firm form. Planning capital is the accumulated diagnostic understanding a firm has built through costly inquiry and operation: understanding of technologies, processes, customers, tools, partners, failures, constraints, and opportunities, together with the capacity to keep learning. It becomes valuable because it helps the firm choose what to investigate, make the question answerable, interpret what happened, and carry what it learned into later investment stages. Building on classical investment theory, R&D models, real-options theory, venture-capital models, classical learning-by-doing, the paper develops a model of investment as staged discovery. The AI and semiconductor frontier makes this asset visible. Firms are being valued and funded for more than the physical capacity they already own. Chips, fabs, data centers, cloud platforms, power commitments, and model systems matter because they carry traces of accumulated learning and because their use generates more learning. They let firms train models, test demand, expose bottlenecks, improve yields, qualify customers, integrate tools, and discover which complements are missing. The current buildout is therefore investment in capacity and in the institutional learning system that makes capacity more valuable over time.The framework explains why production systems, tool systems, research paths, sovereign capability programs, and infrastructure sponsorship belong in the same analysis. They are different institutional forms through which planning capital is accumulated. The paper treats terminal realization value in reduced form and focuses on the discovery process that precedes it: how institutions build capacity, learn from using it, and turn accumulated diagnostic understanding into an advantage in the next round of investment.

title: How Serious Are Experimenter Demand Effects? Evidence and Mitigation Strategies
affiliations: Queen Mary University of London, University of Pittsburgh - Department of Economics and University of Pittsburgh

detail.title: How Serious Are Experimenter Demand Effects? Evidence and Mitigation Strategies

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Experimenter demand effects arise when participants in an experiment or survey distort their behavior in a misguided attempt to please the experimenter by confirming their research hypothesis. Experimental economists have taken the threat of demand effects seriously and have developed an array of best practices to mitigate their influence, as well as bounding techniques to assess their potential impact on inference. We provide an overview of these techniques and summarize recent empirical assessments of the potential threat of experimenter demand. Our main message is that good design is normally sufficient to address demand concerns, and that bounding approaches work well when concerns remain. Existing empirical evidence suggests that the potential impact of experimenter demand is limited.

title: An Informational Rationale for Viewpoint Neutrality in Education
affiliations: and University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy

detail.title: An Informational Rationale for Viewpoint Neutrality in Education

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Consider a society that faces uncertainty about a payoff-relevant state and wants to train students to make correct decisions. In educational institutions, students learn from their teachers, but they also get outside information, and later learn from peers. We show that privately Bayesian actions need not be optimal inputs into social learning: when students' actions reflect teacher-side information that is correlated across peers, observing many such actions can give this information excessive social weight. A social planner may therefore optimally reduce the precision of instruction, inducing students to rely more on outside information before their actions become signals for others, and students can end up better informed despite learning less from their teachers. The case for a precision cap is stronger when peer interaction is homophilous, because same-teacher information is more likely to survive aggregation, and weaker when outside information is itself systematically distorted. This provides an informational rationale for viewpoint neutrality as an institutional policy: it limits the social overrepresentation of correlated teacher-side information when students mostly learn from peers exposed to similar sources.

detail.abstract: Wind energy is indispensable for achieving European climate targets, yet local resistance continues to delay or block projects. One measure increasingly adopted to foster acceptance is the introduction of financial participation and compensation (FPC) schemes. Existing research suggests that such schemes can strengthen acceptance, provided they are designed properly. To date, despite increasing European and national efforts to encourage or require developers to redistribute benefits to local populations, no mapping of FPC regulations or guidelines across Europe exists. We fill this gap by analysing regulations and policy documents in the EU27, Norway, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom, down to the NUTS2 level. The identified 90 schemes across 19 countries and 21 regions are categorised into four types: fixedpayment compensation, profit-based participation, debt-based participation, and equity-based participation. Building on this typology, we analyse and compare schemes and their configurations through the lens of energy justicedistributive (what and how much is shared), recognitional (who is eligible to benefit), and procedural (how are benefits used). Our results highlight a significant variety in compensation amounts and scheme design. For instance, based on our calculations, certain FPC schemes may yield up to 195 times higher payments than others. Building on existing literature, we analyse different scheme designs and their possible impact on local acceptance, thereby supporting policymakers in drafting effective schemes. While the paper focuses on schemes used for onshore wind, findings provide transferable insights for other infrastructures with social impacts and acceptance problems, such as large-scale solar photovoltaics and transmission grids.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the notion of an E-k seminets as a finite incidence structure whose k-semiregular behaviour is not only stated axiomatically, but also encoded, tested and documented through Boolean algebra, incidence matrices, logic circuits and a reproducible computational certificate. The proposed model is positioned between the classical U-k level, in which points, lines and parallel classes are given by axioms, and the G-k level, in which the same structure is interpreted through an auxiliary graph and its local degrees. The E-k level adds a third layer: a binary incidence matrix B, a partition of the line set into k classes, Boolean tests for the M1 and M2 conditions, and a certificate C_B that records whether the candidate object is accepted. The central claim is that every finite U-k semilattice induces an E-k representation, while every accepted E-k object returns an explicit, checkable U-k incidence structure together with a G-k visualization. This makes the model useful for construction, simulation, comparison and archival verification of finite semilattice candidates.

title: Beta for Alpha: Neural Engagement in Financial Trading
affiliations: East China University of Science and Technology, The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics, Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance (SAIF), Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance (SAIF) and University of Michigan at Ann Arbor

detail.title: Beta for Alpha: Neural Engagement in Financial Trading

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The emergence of wearable electroencephalography (EEG) technologies presents new opportunities to identify and quantify neural correlates of decision-making in real-time, financially consequential settings. We report a field study in which we use wearable EEG devices to record brainwave activity from professional day traders during real-world, high-stakes trading. Using these signals, we construct an established psychophysiological Engagement Index (EI), which is defined as beta wave power divided by the sum of alpha and theta wave power, and document clear spike-and-decay patterns around trade execution. Linking EI dynamics to trading performance, we find that more successful trades are preceded by larger EI spikes in the 30 seconds before execution, while baseline or background EI levels have no predictive power and, if anything, are negatively associated with performance. We further show that higher EI is associated with attenuated behavioral biases in trading, including the round number heuristic and the disposition effect.

title: A New Decomposition Approach to Modeling Financial Returns: Conditioning Sign on Magnitude

detail.title: A New Decomposition Approach to Modeling Financial Returns: Conditioning Sign on Magnitude
detail.abstract: Changes in volatility contain valuable information about the likelihood of positive versus negative returns. We propose a new approach to modeling financial returns that exploits this insight by decomposing returns into sign and magnitude (absolute value) components, with magnitude closely related to volatility. The joint distribution used to compute expected returns combines a model for the marginal distribution of magnitude with a model for the distribution of the sign, conditional on the contemporaneous magnitude. Unlike traditional linear predictive regressions, this decomposition framework captures nonlinear predictability in return dynamics. An out-of-sample forecasting evaluation using monthly U.S. stock market excess returns demonstrates substantial statistical and economic gains relative to linear regression and complete subset regression, while delivering performance that is competitive with copula-based return-decomposition methods and other nonlinear benchmarks.

detail.title: Do Renewable Portfolio Standards Deliver Cost-Effective Carbon Abatement?
detail.abstract: The United States' most prevalent climate policies are Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS) that mandate a specified share of electricity come from low-CO2 sources like wind and solar. Using a difference-indifferences style research design, we find that electricity prices are 11% higher seven years after RPS passage. Estimates also indicate that CO2 emissions are 8-17% lower seven years after passage, though they are sensitive to specification (unlike the price estimates). Together, the estimates suggest that the cost per abated CO2 ton ranges from $86-$211. Additionally, there is suggestive evidence that the cost per increment of mandated low-CO2 generation declined after 2010.

detail.title: Central Bank Reserves and the Balance Sheet of Banks
detail.abstract: We introduce a tractable model of the two-tier monetary system with heterogeneous agents and incomplete markets. We use this model to characterize the dynamics of bank lending under general fiscal and monetary policy and derive the welfare optimal level of Central Bank reserves and the optimal interest rate on reserves. We also identify a new risk channel of monetary policy. In the model, banks have a dual role as loan providers and money creators, and cannot fully diversify credit risk. Central Bank reserves are used to settle interbank claims and serve as a safe asset, thereby buffering risks for banks. We show how the Central Bank and the Treasury can implement any desired allocation by setting interest rates, issuing a particular amount of reserves, and imposing taxes, and show that uncoordinated policy responses to shocks by the Central Bank alone may cause sub-optimal outcomes and significant instability.

title: Agricultural Import Competition and Farm Employment: The Role of Mechanization Capacity

detail.title: Agricultural Import Competition and Farm Employment: The Role of Mechanization Capacity
detail.abstract: Agricultural imports into the United States expanded sharply between 2008 and 2022, yet county farm employment did not decline uniformly across agricultural regions. This paper provides evidence consistent with the view that the employment effects of import competition vary systematically with production technology. Using a commodity-specific shift-share Bartik design applied to 2,602 agricultural counties with county and state-year fixed effects, the analysis identifies within-state variation in import exposure from baseline 2007 commodity specialization. The Bartik construction is restricted to three commodity lines, cattle and beef, fruit and tree nuts, and vegetables, for which USDA FATUS provides continuous world-import records. Broad exposure measures incorporating commodity series with zero or near-zero baseline imports produce attenuated and oppositesigned estimates due to explosive log-growth values in contaminated series. The main result is a statistically significant negative employment effect: a one-standard-deviation increase in import exposure is associated with a reduction in log county farm employment of 0.064, approximately 6.4 percent at the county mean. But this aggregate masks a substantively large but imprecisely estimated heterogeneity pattern. High-mechanization grain and field-crop counties show no statistically significant employment response to import competition. Low-mechanization counties, which include specialty crop and labor-intensive livestock systems, show a coefficient of-0.086, equivalent to an 8.3 percent employment reduction, more than three times larger under the step-assigned mechanization classification. The subgroup estimates display a 3.6-fold difference in magnitude, though the gap is imprecisely estimated. A robustness check using only the pre-treatment 2007 machinery baseline yields no gap, but the machinery classification is highly stable across census years (ρ = 0.96; 91.8 % of counties keep the same group) and switching is unrelated to import exposure, suggesting the zero result reflects single-year measurement noise rather than the absence of pre-existing production-system differences. The pattern should be interpreted as suggestive evidence of mechanization-related heterogeneity rather than a definitive structural result. Commodity decomposition shows that statistically significant effects are concentrated in hog production and fruit and tree nut systems, where labor remains difficult to replace through mechanization at the harvest and handling margins, consistent with capital-labor complementarity in these production systems. The results reveal a structural mismatch in trade adjustment policy. The largest employment declines occur in low-mechanization systems dependent on hired labor, while existing adjustment programs, organized around national commodity price triggers and producer-level eligibility criteria, are not well positioned to reach the workers facing the largest employment consequences of agricultural import competition.

title: What the Filings Don't Show Tracing the Credit Behind the AI Build-Out, and the Disclosure Gaps That Hide It

detail.title: What the Filings Don't Show Tracing the Credit Behind the AI Build-Out, and the Disclosure Gaps That Hide It
detail.abstract:
The money behind the AI boom is real; the disclosure architecture that would let anyone price its risks is not. The agentic-AI credit channel-through which bank-and market-sourced capital finances AI infrastructure-leaves investors, regulators, and counterparties without the records they need to see where the risk actually sits. This article asks a simple question: how much of it can an outsider actually see in the public record? It walks through that record in order-from what is clearly visible, to what is visible only in part, to what no filing reveals because no rule requires it-and treats each gap as a testable claim: if the gap is real, the public record should run out at a specific point traceable to a specific missing rule. The evidence is drawn from Shared National Credit data, FDIC call reports, named-bank 10-K filings, business development company marks, SEC N-PORT position data, depreciation schedules, GPU-utilisation proxies, buyer-ROI surveys, residual-value curves, and a cross-jurisdictional inventory of disclosure rules. From the gaps the article derives a short list of disclosure reforms-each one the direct complement of a gap the public record exposes-and characterises the cost of continued opacity in terms of mispriced systemic exposure.

A companion working paper to the parent study (SSRN abstract 6898819). Also deposited at Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20684277.

title: Bounded Paternalism and the Algorithmic Environment: A Liberal Legal Theory of AI-Driven Content Curation under the EU Digital Services Act and the UK Online Safety Act 2023

detail.title: Bounded Paternalism and the Algorithmic Environment: A Liberal Legal Theory of AI-Driven Content Curation under the EU Digital Services Act and the UK Online Safety Act 2023
detail.abstract: When Molly Russell died following months of exposure to algorithmically curated self-harm content, the platforms responsible faced no regulatory obligation to have designed their systems differently. That gap motivates this thesis. Through a comparative analysis of the EU Digital Services Act and the UK Online Safety Act 2023 and drawing on Feinberg's soft paternalism and Raz's perfectionist autonomy, it argues that neither framework alone justifies structural regulation of AI-driven content curation, and develops an original synthesis, bounded paternalism, that does. The standard holds that structural intervention in algorithmic design is justified only where a platform's architecture demonstrably fails to support meaningful autonomous choice, and that failure is established through a transparent, auditable risk-assessment process. Applied comparatively, the DSA emerges as largely well-justified; Article 28(2) DSA as the most philosophically secure provision in either instrument; and the OSA's absence of a structural design obligation triggered by its adult algorithmic risk assessment as a theoretical inconsistency, not a principled limit. The thesis identifies the evidential and institutional conditions that separate legitimate structural regulation from disguised censorship-a distinction the current legislative debate has consistently failed to draw.

The CCJ, through its rulings, has augmented attempts at regional economic integration, and has, to some extent, added to the perception of CARICOM as a potentially supranational institution. title: Innovative Procurement Frameworks for Energy Performance Contracting in the UK Public Sector

detail.title: Innovative Procurement Frameworks for Energy Performance Contracting in the UK Public Sector
detail.abstract: Procurement Frameworks for Energy Performance Contracting (PFEPCs) simplify the process of negotiating, developing and implementing Energy Performance Contracts (EPCs) with Energy Service Companies (ESCOs). This paper analyses their role in promoting the implementation of cost-effective energy efficiency measures in the UK public sector. Compared to conventional approaches to procuring goods and services involving detailed specifications, PFEPCs translate the challenge of upgrading, retrofitting and replacing energy related equipment and infrastructures into required outputs through functional specifications. The innovativeness of specific PFEPCs often lies less in the diffusion of ‘developmental’ innovative energy efficient solutions, although partner bidding approaches create favourable conditions for innovation. However increasing standardisation and bundling prove successful at lowering transaction cost, which enables ESCOs to address projects which would not be considered in the absence of PFEPCs due to high transaction costs. This particular organisational innovation opens the market up to new approaches to implementing cost-effective energy efficiency measures.

detail.abstract: Does institutional design mitigate the biodiversity loss associated with urban land expansion? This study addresses this question by evaluating China's 2018 "Increment-Stock Linkage" (ISL) policy, which mandates that greenfield land quotas be contingent upon the verified redevelopment of existing brownfield land. By integrating monthly county-level bird observation data from the China Bird Report with comprehensive land transaction records, we employ a triple-difference (DDD) empirical strategy that exploits cross-sectional variation in counties' pre-reform reliance on new land development. Our findings reveal a significant reversal in land-biodiversity elasticity: following the reform, elasticity shifts from-0.027 in control counties to +0.009 in treatment counties. We trace this reversal to two complementary channels: at the extensive margin, reduced greenfield conversion preserves edge habitats essential for landscape connectivity; at the intensive margin, the shift toward brownfield redevelopment raises land use efficiency and compels compensatory urban greening within densified cores. detail.abstract: In liquid democracy, the number of accumulated delegations is often taken as a proxy for an agent's influence. However, this intuitive measure ignores the fact that true power stems from pivotality, i.e., the ability to turn a losing coalition into a winning one, which depends on the entire delegation network and the preferences of its participants. We formalize a cooperative simple game from a functional delegation graph and a fixed binary preference profile. Our construction employs a novel vote-loss boundary-severing rule: delegation chains that cross the coalition boundary are severed, and all votes flowing along them are lost. Delegations between agents who share the same preference are discarded, as they cannot affect the outcome. The Shapley value of the induced game then serves as a natural measure of structural voting power. We prove that the game is monotone for acyclic functional graphs, establish Delegation Invariance, and provide a uniqueness theorem that characterizes the vote‑loss rule axiomatically. Analytical results for several canonical topologies (star, alternating and non‑alternating path, middleman, two‑component star, and a balanced binary tree) reveal striking power concentrations that are completely invisible to raw delegation counts. For instance, in a star, the center holds only half the total power, while in a path, the agent farthest from the sink can be entirely powerless. These findings highlight structural power concentrations and may inform the design of fairer delegation mechanisms.

title: Climate Clubs and Positive Carbon Pricing for a Low-Carbon Bretton Woods
affiliations: University of Sussex - Science and Technology Policy Research Unit (SPRU), University of Sussex - Science and Technology Policy Research Unit (SPRU) and University of Sussex

detail.title: Climate Clubs and Positive Carbon Pricing for a Low-Carbon Bretton Woods
detail.abstract: If global average temperature rise is to be limited to 2°C or even 1.5°C below pre-industrial levels this century, we require a paradigm shift in the way we value and exchange mitigations of Greenhouse Gas Emissions (GHGs). Positive carbon pricing shifts the focus from the cost of GHG emissions to the value of mitigating GHG emissions. We hereby propose a climate club governance arrangement based on Article 6 of the Paris Agreement as well as a robust accounting system to create a positive carbon pricing environment. It provides a starting point for modular, scalable and inclusive climate governance arrangements for environmental and social value creation.

title: The Robots Are Coming for Our Safety: The Impact of Automation on U.S. Crime

detail.title: The Robots Are Coming for Our Safety: The Impact of Automation on U.S. Crime
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the causal effect of industrial robot adoption on local crime rates in the United States. While the impact of automation on labor markets is well-documented, its consequences for public safety remain underexplored. Using data on robot adoption from the International Federation of Robotics (IFR) and crime data from the FBI's Uniform Crime Reports (UCR) for 222 Commuting Zones (CZs) from 2001 to 2014, we employ a 2SLS instrumental variable strategy, following Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020). We find that increased exposure to industrial robots leads to a statistically significant and robust increase in property crime rates. This effect is primarily driven by the "economic opportunity channel," as automation reduces local labor market opportunities. In contrast, we find no significant causal effect of robot exposure on violent crime rates. Our robustness checks, including pre-period and spatial placebo tests, confirm the validity of our identification strategy. The findings suggest that the social costs of automation extend beyond the labor market and have direct implications for public safety and policy.

title: Robots Are "Invading" Our Homes: The Impact of Automation on the U.S. Housing Market

detail.title: Robots Are "Invading" Our Homes: The Impact of Automation on the U.S. Housing Market
detail.abstract: This paper examines how industrial automation affects local housing markets in the United States. Using an annual panel of commuting zones from 2010 to 2019, we construct a shiftshare measure of local robot exposure by combining predetermined industry employment shares with industry-level robot adoption. To address the endogeneity of U.S. robot adoption, we instrument local exposure using corresponding adoption patterns in South Korea and Japan. The empirical specifications include region-by-year fixed effects and a rich set of baseline demographic, economic, and housing-market controls. The instrument strongly predicts U.S. robot exposure. On average, robot adoption has no statistically significant effect on house-price growth, median contract-rent growth, or homeownership. However, a one-standard-deviation increase in robot exposure raises annual Fair Market Rent growth by approximately 0.24 percentage points, corresponding to an implied elasticity of about 0.77. The effects also vary across time and local market conditions: automation reduces homeownership during the 2010-2013 recovery period and increases Fair Market Rents during the 2014-2019 expansion, with responses depending on prior house-price growth, housingsupply elasticity, and local labor-market vulnerability. Pre-period and spatial placebo tests provide additional support for the identification strategy. Overall, the findings suggest that automation affects housing markets primarily through rental-market pressures and tenure adjustment rather than through broad changes in property values, highlighting an important distributional consequence of technological change.

detail.abstract: This paper describes a specific instance of the growth axiom established for the Global Flow System in the cycle's first chapter: the layer in which the tension of a saturated field turns toward the next extensive opening. That layer is computation. The argument reads the rapid accumulation of capital around artificial intelligence not as pathology but as an energy balance. Overheated flow seeks a channel of release; within a closed space every channel is destructive, and only extensive space, now the Solar System, is not. The financing wall and the selfreferential vortex are not rival readings but two faces of the same overheating. In this picture the crash is not the refutation of exit but its condition, a present instance of the law of expansionary captivity: the question is not whether it will come, but what remains afterward and where. Computation is the model of the gate because in it the vortex and the exit are two directions of a single capital structure, because in the wider conversion chain (energy, compute, intelligence, conditioning) it is the middle conversion, and because its three columns (classical compute, artificial intelligence, quantum) show that the threshold is half built. The paper treats the valve, the measuring layer, and the three flow constitutions as the computational-layer instances of concepts set out in the first chapter, and treats the material asymmetry, the shared principle that links ochre and compute, as the reason computation is the industry that exits.

detail.abstract: We study short-term reversal in Chinese A-shares on a fully traceable, point-in-time, delisting-inclusive database, using a monthly signal based on the past three months of returns that skips the most recent trading week. Over 2014:05-2026:02 (142 months), an equal-weighted loser-minus-winner long-short portfolio earns 1.72% per month (Newey-West 𝑡 = 3.64) and rises nearly monotonically across signal deciles (8 of 9 adjacent steps increasing). The effect is not absorbed by standard controls: a CH-3-style factor model leaves an alpha of 1.46% per month (𝑡 = 3.33), and Fama-MacBeth regressions controlling for size, earnings-to-price, Amihud illiquidity, and industry retain a significant reversal coefficient (𝑡 = 3.51). These risk-adjustment results survive multiple testing: under a Romano-Wolf step-down across the factor-model and Fama-MacBeth specification families, the featured specifications retain familywise-adjusted 𝑝-values of 0.0024 and 0.007, every one of the sixteen Fama-MacBeth specifications survives at adjusted 𝑝 ≤ 0.014, and all five factor-model specifications at 𝑝 ≤ 0.0032; the orthogonality also holds against the official Liu-Stambaugh-Yuan factors (alpha 1.88% per month, 𝑡 = 2.81, over the 2014-2021 overlap). Reversal is also not merely the volatility/lottery/turnover complex in disguise: when idiosyncratic volatility, the MAX lottery measure, turnover, beta, and momentum are measured over a window that does not overlap the signal-formation window, they leave the reversal coefficient intact (Fama-MacBeth 𝑡 = 4.3; three-factor alpha 1.32% per month, 𝑡 = 3.1). Such controls appear to absorb reversal only when measured over the same window as the signal-a mechanical artifact that vanishes monotonically as the control window is separated from it (§6.6). The tradable claim is weaker on every margin we examine. The long-only loser portfolio's excess over an equal-weighted universe is 0.25% per month (net-versus-net), loses single-test significance beyond 10-30 bps of proportional cost, and-measured against an investable cap-weighted index, the relevant opportunity cost-is economically large (about 1% per month) but statistically insignificant (𝑡 ≈ 1.5). After a max-𝑡 correction across 72 strategy-selection candidates the zero-cost excess is not significant (adjusted 𝑝 = 0.288), whether the long side is the loser half or the extreme loser decile. Returns concentrate in less-liquid small-and mid-cap stocks, and the long-short is materially lower in later subsamples (no formally identified trend). We read A-share short-term reversal as a genuine cross-sectional regularity-robust to standard factors and to a stock's pre-existing volatility/lottery/turnover character-that is nonetheless economically constrained as a trade: predictability and tradability diverge once multiplicity and frictions are treated explicitly.

detail.abstract: India's digital commerce market, valued at approximately USD 159 billion and growing at nearly 16% annually, has outpaced the governance structures meant to protect the citizens who use it. Government helpline data shows e-commerce grievances more than doubling between 2020-21 and 2023-24, while existing consumer protection law leaves consumers to navigate fragmented liability between platforms, vendors, and logistics partners, with no automatic remedy for common harms such as failed transactions, misrepresented products, or delayed refunds. This paper proposes a regulatory framework for large consumer-facing digital platforms in India, grounded in five foundational principles-single-interface liability, payment custody, consumer asymmetry, price integrity, and consumer convenience-and operationalised through thirteen nonwaivable consumer rights spanning the full purchase journey. Central to the framework is a shift from complaint-driven to self-executing protection: platforms act automatically on data they already hold, rather than requiring consumers to pursue remedy through human-mediated, and often inconsistent, complaint processes. The framework further extends direct protections to delivery agents, whose safety is put at risk by platform delivery-speed incentives, and proposes a graduated enforcement regimeculminating in the power to suspend a platform's transaction gateway-backed by a public Platform Performance Index and real-time regulatory data access. Developed from citizen observation rather than institutional research, this paper offers both a normative argument for consumer-first platform governance and a concrete design for implementing it within India's Digital India programme.

detail.abstract:
Background: The NHS is responsible for approximately 4% of UK greenhouse gas emissions, with patient travel to general practice (GP) appointments accounting for 10% of the total NHS carbon footprint. Digital health technologies offer a potential pathway to reduce these emissions, yet comprehensive national-level evidence quantifying the climate, air quality, and economic co-benefits of replacing in-person GP consultations with virtual alternatives has been lacking.

Methods: We analysed NHS Digital data on monthly GP appointments in England (September 2018–January 2025) by type (in-person, telephone, and online) and region. CO₂ and air pollutant (NOₓ, PM2.5, PM₁₀) emissions were estimated from national emission factors and damage cost valuations. Benefit–cost ratios compared the value of quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) gained from primary care against total costs (emissions, NHS financial, and patient costs). Three future scenarios to 2045 were modelled: accelerated digital transition, continuation of 2024 volumes, and log-scale trend extrapolation. Deterministic sensitivity analysis assessed the robustness of the health economic findings.

Findings: Virtual consultations generated cumulative net CO₂ savings of approximately 767,833 tonnes nationally (range 461,000–1,075,000 in sensitivity analyses), equivalent to removing 167,000 passenger cars for one year. Online appointments increased more than ten-fold to over 2 million monthly by 2025. Cumulative NOₓ emissions from in-person travel exceeded 3 million kg. Benefit–cost ratios were positive across all scenarios, at approximately 3.0 (range 1.9–4.8) per £1 spent (QALYs valued at £20,000) and 10.3 (range 6.7–16.7) per £1 spent (QALYs valued at £70,000).

Interpretation: Scaling virtual GP consultations in England can deliver substantial climate, air quality, and economic co-benefits while maintaining positive benefit–cost ratios. Realising these gains requires addressing digital exclusion to ensure sustainability and health equity progress together. These findings support the NHS net-zero strategy and the 2025 NHS 10-Year Plan ambition for digitally enabled primary care.

Background: Early identification and timely intervention are critical for malignant hepatic tumors to optimize patient prognosis. Misdiagnosis of benign hepatic space-occupying lesions (HSOLs) as malignancies may trigger overtreatment, imposing unnecessary financial burdens and physical risks on patients. In Xinjiang, China, its vast geographic area and uneven distribution of medical resources contribute to significant inter-regional discrepancies in diagnostic capabilities for HSOLs among physicians. The present study aimed to develop an artificial intelligence-assisted ultrasound diagnostic system for HSOLs (AI-US-DS-HSOL) in order to support ultrasound practitioners across diverse regions.

Methods: A multicenter investigation enrolled patients from ten hospitals across eight Xinjiang prefectures. Retrospective clinical and ultrasonographic data (static and dynamic clips) were consecutively collected between April 2012 and March 2025 from 7,934 patients diagnosed with ten HSOL subtypes, including cystic echinococcosis (CE1–CE5), alveolar echinococcosis, hepatic cyst, hepatic hemangioma, and liver cancer. Deep learning architectures comprising LACTNet, YOLOv10-EfficientFormerV2, RepViT, and PPLiteSeg-STDC1 were utilized as backbones to construct AI-US-DS-HSOL, integrating liver parenchymal segmentation, focal lesion detection, lesion delineation, and pathological subtype classification in a unified pipeline. Real-world diagnostic capabilities of sonographers from 13 prefectures of Xinjiang were systematically assessed for the first time, enrolling over 100 practicing ultrasound physicians. Prospectively acquired ultrasound images from three hospitals between April and October 2025 were reserved as the external validation cohort to comparatively benchmark diagnostic performance between AI-US-DS-HSOL and physicians.

Findings: A total of 45,124 ultrasound images were split into training, internal validation, and internal test subsets for model development. The overall classification accuracy of internal validation set reached 0∙898, with a macro-averaged area under the curve (AUC) of 0∙975. Macro-averaged specificity, sensitivity, and F1-score were 0∙880, 0∙880, and 0∙879, respectively, with tightly aligned high values across these metrics. The overall accuracy of the internal test set improved to 0∙904 alongside a macro-averaged AUC of 0∙977. The corresponding macro-specificity, macro-sensitivity, and macro-F1 were 0∙891, 0∙889, and 0∙889. In binary discrimination between echinococcal and non-echinococcal liver lesions, AI-US-DS-HSOL achieved an AUC of 0∙955, sensitivity of 0∙737, specificity of 0∙955, F1-score of 0∙836, and Youden’s Index of 0∙691. For ten-category differential diagnosis of all enrolled HSOL subtypes, the model yielded macro-AUC of 0∙847, sensitivity of 0∙807, specificity of 0∙983, F1-score of 0∙817, and Youden’s Index of 0∙790. The overall diagnostic accuracy for the 130 participating physicians was 0∙635, stratified as 0∙662 for junior, 0∙625 for intermediate and 0∙621 for senior practitioners. Most of them were inferior to the standalone performance of AI-US-DS-HSOL. After accessing the AI auxiliary prompts, the diagnostic accuracy of 110 reassessed physicians rose significantly to 0∙794 (junior), 0∙803 (intermediate), and 0∙839 (senior) (p<0∙001).

Interpretation: AI-US-DS-HSOL provides a propagable auxiliary diagnostic tool for HSOL management of regional healthcare facilities in Xinjiang, and it enhances diagnostic capabilities in primary care hospitals.

title: Digital Transformation in Accounting and Financial Consultancy Firms and the Future of Accounting Jobs

detail.title: Digital Transformation in Accounting and Financial Consultancy Firms and the Future of Accounting Jobs
detail.abstract: Purpose. This paper examines how digital transformation is reshaping accounting and financial consultancy firms and, in turn, redefining the future of accounting jobs. It integrates evidence on cloud accounting, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning, robotic process automation (RPA), blockchain, and advanced data analytics with a primary, multi-region empirical study of 412 accounting professionals and twelve in-depth interviews. Design/methodology/approach. A mixed-methods sequential design was adopted. A structured online survey (administered between September 2025 and February 2026) measured twelve latent constructs spanning digital adoption, productivity, job redesign, displacement anxiety, upskilling intention, advisory orientation, and ethical concerns. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlation, ordinary-least-squares regression, and moderation tests in SPSS and Stata. Twelve semi-structured interviews with senior practitioners were thematically coded to triangulate findings. Findings. Digital adoption intensity is a strong, positive predictor of perceived productivity (β = .42, p < .001) and advisory orientation (β = .36, p < .001). Cloud accounting and data analytics show the highest adoption maturity (M = 3.80 and 3.30 respectively, on a 1-5 scale); AI/ML adoption is rising rapidly but uneven; blockchain remains embryonic. Job displacement anxiety is moderate and concentrated in junior and routine roles, while upskilling intention is uniformly high. The data support a profession-wide pivot from compliance-centric to advisory-centric work, with new hybrid job archetypes such as the accounting data scientist, AI audit specialist, and ESG reporting lead emerging across all firm-size bands and regions. Originality/value. The study contributes one of the largest cross-regional empirical pictures of digital transformation in the accounting profession published in the 2020-2026 window. It integrates technology adoption, work-design, and labour-market lenses into a single conceptual model, validates it on primary data, and translates the findings into a forward-looking taxonomy of accounting jobs through 2030. Implications are drawn for firm leaders, regulators, educators, and accounting professionals navigating the AI-augmented profession.

detail.abstract: Self-interested strategic (opportunistic) behavior can quietly undermine well-intended policies in healthcare. One prominent setting is hospital discharge: clinicians may strategically shorten length of stay (LoS) to reduce costs or meet throughput targets, prioritizing financial objectives over clinical considerations. A central open question is thus identifying whether and which physicians systematically exhibit such strategic behavior. Detecting such behavior is difficult because strategic intent can be confounded by patient self-selection, physician diagnostic ability, and general decision errors. Also, the counterfactual decision needed to establish such strategic behavior is unobserved (i.e., what the physician would have done under different incentives). To address these challenges, we develop a systematic three-step AI framework with a Deconfounding Hierarchical Latent model that uses counterfactual modeling to separate incentive-driven channels (e.g., payer types) from non-incentive factors and confounders. Using Maryland sepsis inpatient data, we flag about 9.1% of physicians as suspiciously strategic: their predicted discharge decisions systematically shorten LoS and are unusually susceptible to incentive changes after accounting for likely confounders. We validate the findings using Healthgrades physician reviews. Extensive experiments show that our framework addresses the core methodological challenges and consistently outperforms benchmarks that only capture general decision errors. We further document heterogeneity in the prevalence of such strategic behavior across patient severity, physician experience levels, hospital types, and hospital revenue-cap pressure. Overall, our study offers a scalable "triage" tool that helps identify strategic physicians for targeted, case-specific follow-up review. We also offer actionable implications for designing effective systems that curb opportunistic behavior without penalizing legitimate decisions.

detail.abstract: This paper examines eco-product adoption, pricing, and environmental performance under a Performance-Price Ratio (PPR) framework. We begin with an experimental study in the context of washing machines to assess whether PPR provides a plausible behavioral foundation for modeling green product choices. The results show that the PPR of eco-products is lower than that of standard products and significantly predicts purchase intentions. We also identify two consumer segments based on environmental awareness and show that these segments evaluate eco-products differently: high-awareness consumers perceive eco-products similarly to standard products, whereas low-awareness consumers assign lower value to eco-products. Motivated by these findings, we develop a PPR-based consumer choice model and embed it into a manufacturer pricing problem with standard and eco products. We then conduct a computational study to examine how incentives that reduce the marginal cost of the eco product interact with consumer heterogeneity and product characteristics to shape adoption and environmental outcomes. The analysis shows that the PPR framework can capture key demand and pricing dynamics and reproduce many of the incentive-related patterns emphasized in the literature. These results suggest that the PPR framework provides a plausible and tractable basis for analyzing ecoproduct adoption and the effectiveness of environmental incentive policies.

title: Algorithmic Compatibility and the Market Selection of Pricing Technologies

detail.title: Algorithmic Compatibility and the Market Selection of Pricing Technologies
detail.abstract: This article studies how market selection across pricing algorithms can soften product-market competition. Firms choose between a competitive algorithm and a compatibility-based algorithm. Compatible algorithms sustain high prices only when they meet compatible rivals, generating a critical adoption threshold. Common vendors and shared benchmarks lower this threshold, whereas compatibility restrictions can eliminate the basin of attraction. The model shows that the markets in which compatibility-based pricing is most harmful are also those in which private selection most favors it. With heterogeneous adoption costs, low-cost adopters can create critical mass, inducing broader diffusion and motivating targeted regulation.

title: Learn now or wait: Intertemporal Bundling with Costly Consumer Search
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management

detail.title: Learn now or wait: Intertemporal Bundling with Costly Consumer Search

publicationDetails.journalName: HKUST Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study intertemporal bundling when consumers face uncertainty about future consumption. A monopolist sells a current product and a future product over two periods. Before committing in period 1, the consumer may pay to learn her valuation of the future product, while waiting reveals it for free in period 2. This setting captures subscription-style contracts common in practice, where consumers must commit in advance to future usage. Under separate selling, the option to wait makes early information acquisition weakly dominated, so the seller cannot induce early search. Intertemporal bundling changes this logic by linking current and future consumption, thereby exploiting strategic consumers' "learn-now-or-wait" behavior. In equilibrium, low-valuation consumers reject, intermediate consumers acquire information early and then decide, and sufficiently high-valuation consumers commit without searching. 

We show that bundling can strictly outperform separate selling even under independent valuations, without any correlation-based pooling motive. The key force is dynamic: bundling reshapes when consumers become informed and when they commit. At the same time, bundling profitability reflects two forces. When search costs are moderate, a dynamic search-inducement effect drives the gain. When search costs are high and no consumer searches, bundling may still outperform separate selling through a static prior-based pooling or commitment effect. We further examine fallback bundling and and menu bundling, which preserve the option of selling product 2 upon bundling, and they differ in whether the seller sells product 1 alone. In a uniform benchmark, we characterize behavior and profits in closed form and illustrate how bundling performance varies with search costs and valuation distributions.

title: Add-On Pricing and Bundling under Sequential Search
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management

detail.title: Add-On Pricing and Bundling under Sequential Search

publicationDetails.journalName: HKUST Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Add-on services are ubiquitous-from airlines charging for checked bags to software companies selling basic versions with premium features at extra cost; yet firms struggle with whether to bundle those extras or keep them separate. We consider a monopoly model in which a base product and a complementary add-on are sold to consumers who must incur search costs to learn their personal valuations. Consumers rationally decide how much to learn about the add-on before purchasing. We derive equilibrium search strategies under separate add-on pricing versus pure bundling. 

Bundling the add-on with the base not only changes the prices paid but also what consumers know when they purchase: bundling induces high-valuation consumers to buy with incomplete information, capturing more revenue from the add-on and potentially increasing profit when search costs are moderate. Our analysis also compares different search sequences (base-first vs. add-on-first). Bundling can reverse the consumer's search order when the add-on is sufficiently variable. We extend our analysis to multiple add-ons and show that bundling's profit advantage tends to increase as more add-ons are offered, highlighting bundling as a valuable demand-management tool in multi-product settings. Moreover, when supply is limited, bundling serves as a demand-management tool by prioritizing higher-value transactions and maximizing revenue from scarce capacity.

title: Keeping Options Open: Optimal Sequential Search with Reservation Costs
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management

detail.title: Keeping Options Open: Optimal Sequential Search with Reservation Costs

publicationDetails.journalName: HKUST Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study a sequential search problem in which previously inspected options can be revisited, but doing so requires paying a per-period reservation (or maintenance) cost. This simple friction fundamentally alters the structure of optimal search policies. We establish that optimal policies are characterized by threshold rules, but-unlike the classic costless-recall model of Weitzman (1979)-the optimal stopping region can exhibit a double reservation value (DRV) structure with two distinct thresholds. We show that this two-threshold behavior arises from two orthogonal mechanisms: (i) a fee-driven mechanism induced solely by the presence of positive recall costs, and (ii) a distribution-driven mechanism arising from non-regular payoff distributions. The former occurs even under standard regularity conditions (e.g., increasing failure rate), while the latter persists even in the absence of recall costs. 

Our analysis delivers sharp conditions under which indexability holds and when it fails. In particular, we demonstrate that even small positive recall costs can break the path-independence of optimal search, generating endogenous history dependence despite identical option distributions. At the same time, we identify environments in which a simple index policy continues to apply. Finally, we show that the model provides a unifying framework encompassing a range of existing search environments, including free recall, no recall, costly recall, and uncertain recall. The results highlight how maintaining flexibility during search creates new tradeoffs between exploration and retention, with implications for optimal decision making, market design, and consumer search.

title: The Strategic Octopus Index (SOI): A Self-Calibrating Quantitative Model for Measuring Institutional Coherence and Geopolitical Effectiveness

detail.title: The Strategic Octopus Index (SOI): A Self-Calibrating Quantitative Model for Measuring Institutional Coherence and Geopolitical Effectiveness

detail.abstract:
Why do resource-rich states and regional blocs consistently underperform strategically? This paper argues the root cause is not a scarcity of capabilities, but a failure of organic coordination between decision-making centres and their operational arms.

We introduce the Strategic Octopus Index (SOI) — a self-calibrating quantitative model that measures strategic coherence across any state or regional bloc through three analytically distinct components: Head Efficiency (R*), Arm Coordination (L*), and the Reflection Coefficient (C*). The latter is grounded in the Global Reflection Economic Theory (GRE), which treats institutional trust as a measurable economic asset rather than a soft political objective.

The model's defining methodological feature is Hierarchical Simplification: component weights (α, β, γ) are derived automatically from system data via inverse-weighting, satisfying α + β + γ = 1 by mathematical necessity. A formal proof of Monotone Stability demonstrates that improving any single component reduces its weight and raises the weights of weaker components — penalising narrow specialisation and rewarding structural balance.

The paper provides: (i) a fully notated mathematical framework with proofs of unbiasedness and stability; (ii) complete variable definitions including the Volatility Weighting Coefficient δ; (iii) objective calibration of D_q via World Bank WGI (Government Effectiveness × 0.6 + Regulatory Quality × 0.4); (iv) a comparative application to seven international systems (EU, ASEAN, Mercosur, United States, Singapore, African Union); (v) a sensitivity analysis (±10–30%) confirming robustness; (vi) a long-run empirical validation series for the European Union (2012–2026) tracking SOI against five major documented structural events; and (vii) a systematic comparison with WGI, GCI, FSI, LPI, and CPI, identifying SOI's unique prescriptive capacity.

SOI's core contribution is not merely diagnostic but prescriptive: self-derived weights automatically identify the highest-leverage intervention point — build the head when α dominates, coordinate the arms when β dominates, invest in reflexive trust when γ lags.

title: Interfirm Cooperation and Capital Market Performance: Automated Textual Analysis of Voluntary Disclosures in Form 10-Ks
affiliations: , Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg and Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg

detail.title: Interfirm Cooperation and Capital Market Performance: Automated Textual Analysis of Voluntary Disclosures in Form 10-Ks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors report there are no competing interests to declare.

detail.abstract: Interfirm cooperations (IFCs) are non-equity-based arrangements—frequently with corporate partners formed across industry boundaries—that have thrived in volatile and uncertain business environments recently. Despite their importance, IFCs are not subject to mandatory disclosure requirements. Drawing on signalling theory, we show how managers can achieve beneficial capital market effects by voluntarily providing IFC-related information. Using automated textual analysis, we extract IFC-related disclosure elements from firms’ Form 10-K filings and construct a novel metric to capture the extent of such information. We then examine how this disclosure metric relates to the various capital market performance indicators of our sample firms. Our empirical results reveal inverted U-shaped associations between the extent of these disclosures and firms’ market value and trading volume. We further find U-shaped associations between the extent of such disclosures and firms’ cost of equity capital and bid-ask spread. Our study thus demonstrates the value relevance of voluntary IFC-related disclosures and their usefulness to investors in decision-making. Considering the identified non-linear relationships, we emphasise the importance for firms to strike a strategic balance regarding the extent of their voluntary IFC-related disclosures in order to maximise their capital market performance while minimising proprietary costs and information overload for investors.

title: Madisonian Nonprofit Law
affiliations: New York University School of Law

detail.title: Madisonian Nonprofit Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: NYU School of Law, Public Law Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: NYU School of Law, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The nonprofit sector is often described as a counterweight to the state. But how exactly do nonprofit organizations check and balance public power? This essay argues that nonprofits constrain government not only by confronting agencies as adversaries but also by supplementing public services and by insinuating themselves into the state’s administrative apparatus as indispensable contractors. The essay also identifies a previously overlooked way in which nonprofit organizations—from amateur sports leagues to hierarchical religious orders—socialize active citizens and stabilize political institutions: by teaching the distinctively democratic “art of losing,” without which peaceful transitions of power become impossible.

The essay’s framework exposes deep tensions in nonprofit law and policy. The charitable contribution deduction, for example, strengthens nonprofits’ ability to resist government pressure but may undermine civic skill-building by encouraging professionalization over volunteer governance. The Johnson Amendment—which prohibits section 501(c)(3) organizations from endorsing candidates for public office—facilitates political depolarization but constrains political mobilization. Limits on the commercial activities of nonprofit organizations maintain a degree of separation between the nonprofit and for-profit sectors—strengthening one aspect of the intersectoral system of checks and balances—but potentially require nonprofits to become even more reliant on government. State attorney general oversight of the nonprofit sector bolsters donor confidence but also creates risks of ideologically motivated enforcement.

 A “Madisonian” perspective on nonprofit law—one that foregrounds the role of nonprofits in the intersectoral system of checks and balances—can help legislators and practitioners weigh tradeoffs among competing democratic values. A Madisonian perspective also reveals that interbranch and intersectoral checks and balances are co-constitutive: traditional Madisonian institutions depend on norms cultivated by the nonprofit sector, while nonprofits rely on legislative and judicial protection to counterbalance executive power. In this way, Madisonian nonprofit law both builds upon and sustains Madisonian constitutional law.

title: Does Everyone Using AI Mean No One Wins? How AI Affects Competitive Advantage
affiliations: Mindanao State University-General Santos, Philippines, Mindanao State University- General Santos, Mindanao State University- General Santos, Mindanao State University- General Santos, Mindanao State University- General Santos, Mindanao State University- General Santos and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Does Everyone Using AI Mean No One Wins? How AI Affects Competitive Advantage
detail.abstract: Over the last few years, the fundamentals of running a business have changed. Business processes rely on available data, and making the right decision involves working closely together with AI. First Generation AI relied on historical data sets to model predictions that would inform smart decision-making. Companies that adopted this AI early gained the competitive edge and were able to capitalize faster on the insights. But today, AI software is widespread and easily accessible. This paper answers the big question: Is AI still the competitive edge? Or has it become a fundamental necessity, much like the internet? Even with greater accessibility, having access to AI is hardly enough. Firms with the right combination of these are much more likely to thrive and gain a competitive edge. AI changes the entire basis of competition. Today, it demands unlimited data, swift, accurate responses, and the ability to learn and improve. It no longer matters how big an organization is. The difference between the most digitally and as a result, AI-enabled firms may soon be so big that it is impossible to catch up.

detail.abstract: When patients experience an opioid use disorder (OUD)-related hospitalization or emergency visit, the transition back to ambulatory care represents a critical window for initiating medication-assisted treatment (MAT). Yet only about one in five patients initiates MAT within 30 days. We examine whether timely primary care follow-up facilitates treatment initiation and identify the care delivery mechanisms through which this e!ect operates. Using claims data covering more than 111,000 patients, we find that follow-up within seven days increases MAT initiation (IV-adjusted OR = 1.11) and is associated with improved long-term adherence (baseline-adjusted OR = 1.17) and lower relapse risk (baseline-adjusted OR = 0.82), with convergent estimates from propensity score matching and Heckman selection sensitivity. An instrumental variable approach reveals that addressing selection roughly cuts the estimated MAT-initiation lift from 33% to 11% (OR = 1.33 vs. 1.11), underscoring the importance of addressing selection into follow-up care. We examine two mechanisms: telehealth moderates the relationship through a substitution effect, functioning as an alternative pathway when in-person access is limited; non-pharmacologic treatments mediate approximately 18% of the follow-up-to-initiation relationship, serving as enablers of pharmacologic uptake. Together, these findings reframe post-acute transitions as a care delivery design problem and identify three operational levers for discharge protocol design: stratifying patients by accessibility profile, routing them to a single care modality rather than layering modalities, and sequencing supportive services as on-ramps to pharmacologic treatment. The asymmetric magnitudes of selection and causal effect imply that current discharge protocols disproportionately reach patients who would initiate treatment regardless of system design, a finding with direct implications for which transition-design interventions can plausibly expand treatment uptake.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence governance debates are often framed as a conflict between ethical oversight and technological innovation. This paper argues that the debate is fundamentally mischaracterized. Furthermore, the central challenge is how to govern digital infrastructures whose underlying design logic evolved outside democratic and regulatory processes.  Drawing comparisons to the historical regulation of finance and energy sectors in Europe, the paper examines why existing governance models may be insufficient for digital and AI infrastructures. Unlike traditional infrastructures, today’s digital systems emerged from privately developed market products that later became socially indispensable systems shaping communication, economic activity, and decision-making processes. As a result, policymakers are increasingly tasked with regulating infrastructures whose internal architectures they have no insight into. The paper acknowledges that the “Ethics by Design”-framework solves some challenges and argues that complimentary measures are needed. It proposes that more effective governance may require interdisciplinary collaboration between technical experts, policymakers, and applied ethicists capable of identifying how infrastructural design itself produces ethical and democratic challenges.
AI assistance was used in the preparation of this work.

title: Generative AI-Style Analyst Writing, Narrative Convergence, and Market Response

detail.title: Generative AI-Style Analyst Writing, Narrative Convergence, and Market Response
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether generative AI-style writing changes the information content of sell-side analyst reports. Sell-side reports are valuable not only because they contain forecasts, recommendations, and target prices, but also because analysts provide written justifications and interpretations of firm news. A common AI writing technology may therefore affect the incremental information conveyed by analyst research even when it lowers production costs. I test this idea using 93,055 Korean analyst reports issued between 2015 and 2025. Comparing reports written about the same firm event, I find that reports are more similar in semantic content and report structure when the covering analysts have higher prior exposure to AI-style writing. High-exposure report events are also followed by higher abnormal trading value and greater intraday range volatility, especially for stocks with high prior analyst coverage and low pre-event liquidity. The evidence suggests that generative AI-style writing is associated with a different market reaction to analyst information: greater trading activity and range-based volatility, alongside more standardized narratives from otherwise independent analysts.

detail.abstract: A cryptographically relevant quantum computer would expose roughly a quarter of the circulating Bitcoin supply, approximately five million coins under a strict definition, including the 1.1 million BTC associated with the Patoshi mining cluster. The Bitcoin community is debating whether to soft-fork the protocol to disable spending from exposed-key addresses, a quantum sunset, at the cost of forcing dormant holders to identify themselves on-chain. A recent proposal by Robinson (2026) introduces Provable Address-Control Timestamps (PACTs), a commitment scheme allowing holders to silently pre-commit today to a hash redeemable via a post-quantum-secure proof if a sunset is later enacted. The construction is technically elegant; the economic, governance, and adoption questions surrounding it are unaddressed. This paper closes that gap. The central conclusion is that the PACT design is the correct framework and should be standardized in the form Robinson proposes; the analysis identifies an additional institutional design problem, pooling privacy costs across holders, whose solution would complete the protective coverage the proposal is designed to deliver. We provide a fresh cohort analysis of vulnerable Bitcoin via BigQuery; a five-criterion framework applied to six policy options; a game-theoretic model of voluntary PACT adoption that identifies an inversion result, namely that under a convex privacy-cost specification the largest dormant holders are the population least likely to commit voluntarily, a feature of any voluntary mechanism rather than a defect in the PACT design; a regulatory analysis of three CRQC-arrival scenarios; and an open-source reference implementation. The implication is that early standardization of the commitment format, paired with an institutional service that pools privacy costs, is the highest-leverage action available to the Bitcoin community today.
